'''''Euphorbia maculata''''', known as '''spotted spurge''', '''prostrate spurge''' (not to be confused with ''[[Euphorbia prostrata]]''), '''milk purslane''', or '''spotted sandmat''',  is a fast-growing [[annual plant]] in the family [[Euphorbiaceae]]. It is native to North America, where it is generally considered a common weed. It can be found in disturbed soils such as garden beds, along railroad tracks, and in the cracks of sidewalks.<ref>Weakley, A.S., and Southeastern Flora Team. 2024. Flora of the southeastern United States Web App. University of North Carolina Herbarium, North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, U.S.A. fsus.ncbg.unc.edu Accessed Oct 24, 2024</ref> It has become a common [[introduced species]] throughout the world, including Europe, Japan, Korea, Australia, and New Zealand.<ref>{{GBIF|id=3067119|taxon=''Euphorbia maculata''|access-date=4 December 2022}}</ref>

[[File:Prostrate spurge.jpg|thumb|Prostrate spurge growing on disturbed soil]]
It grows in sunny locations and a variety of soils, and functions as a [[pioneer species]] in [[ecological succession]]. The sap of this plant is a mild skin irritant and can cause a rash in some people.<ref>{{cite web |title=Prostrate Spurge |url=http://www.colostate.edu/Depts/CoopExt/4DMG/Weed/spurge.htm |website=CSU/Denver County Extension |access-date=18 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150922192731/http://www.colostate.edu/Depts/CoopExt/4DMG/Weed/spurge.htm |archive-date=22 September 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The milky sap of plants in genus ''Euphorbia'' is poisonous and considered carcinogenic.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Candice |title=Plants That Cause Skin Irritation |url=http://web.extension.illinois.edu/jsw/downloads/PlantsThatCauseSkinIrritationFactSheet.pdf |website=University of Illinois Extension |access-date=18 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150701201550/http://web.extension.illinois.edu/jsw/downloads/PlantsThatCauseSkinIrritationFactSheet.pdf |archive-date=1 July 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Description==
As originally described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]], ''Euphorbia maculata'' is an herbaceous plant with small, oblong opposite leaves. The leaves are pilose, or covered in small thin hairs, and generally have a [[Crenation|crenate]] (scalloped) edge. Each leaf is marked with a small brown spot in the center, giving the plant its common name.<ref>C. Linnaeus, ''Species Plantarum'', Vol. 1, London, 1753, pp. 455.</ref>

''Euphorbia maculata'' is typically prostrate, with specimens rarely reaching as high as {{convert|30|cm}}. The stems spread out in a mat along the ground with each stem rarely greater than {{convert|45|cm}} long. The [[leaf|leaves]] are oval but rather elongate, up to {{convert|3|cm}} long. The [[cyathium|cyathia]], bisexual reproductive structures unique to plants in the genus, are very small, with four white petal-like appendages that are sometimes pink.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Webster |first=Grady L. |date=1967 |title=The Genera of Euphorbiaceae in the Southeastern United States |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43782494 |journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=363–430 |doi=10.5962/p.185727 |jstor=43782494 |issn=0004-2625|doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Euphorbia maculata'' flowers in the summer. These flowers develop in clusters near the axillary bud, they are small and leaf-like, with a red calyx. Upon blooming they have lobed, white to pink petals.<ref name=":0">"Euphorbia maculata (Spotted Spurge): Minnesota Wildflowers". ''www.minnesotawildflowers.info''. Retrieved 2024-10-24.</ref>

''Euphorbia maculata'' develops a small, 3-lobed fruit. This fruit, like the rest of the plant, is covered in fine, soft hairs. Each lobe is a capsule that contains a single seed. The seeds are small, oblong, and white to light brown. The surface is uneven and covered in little divots.<ref name=":0" />

''Euphorbia maculata'' is similar to ''[[Euphorbia prostrata]]'', but that species has shorter leaves that are more rounded at the tips. It may occasionally be confused with ''[[Euphorbia serpens]]'' but this taxon has very short and rounded leaves and larger (but still inconspicuous) cyathia.{{cn|date=December 2024}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Euphorbia maculata'' is considered native to all of the continental United States according to the United States Department of Agriculture.<ref>"USDA Plants Database". ''plants.usda.gov''. Retrieved 2024-10-23.</ref> Spotted Spurge has been naturalized in much of the world. This includes South America, Australia, Asia, parts of Africa, and throughout Europe.<ref name=":1">"Spotted spurge - Euphorbia maculata (Taxonomy, Characteristics, Symbolism, Images, Toxic)". ''PictureThis''. Retrieved 2024-10-24.</ref>

''Euphorbia maculata'' is commonly found along roadsides, in the cracks and crevasses of sidewalks, and throughout North America. It grows in sunny and arid areas without much shade.<ref>Park, K.; Lee, H.; Jang, B.-K.; Cho, J.-S. Dormancy Characteristics of ''Euphorbia maculata'' L. Seeds and Strategies for Their Effective Germination. ''Horticulturae'' '''2023''', ''9'', 990. <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.3390/horticulturae9090990</nowiki></ref> Spotted spurge grows well in coarse soils, such as sand or gravel, but can also be found growing in compacted soils and areas with poor soil. It grows best in conditions in full sun.<ref name=":0" />

== Uses ==
''Euphorbia maculata'' is understood throughout most of North America as a weed, however it is used in Asia as a medicinal plant. The species possesses [[triterpenoid]]s that when medicinally applied, have anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative properties.<ref>Sun, Y.; Gao, L.-l.; Tang, M.-y.; Feng, B.-m.; Pei, Y.-h.; Yasukawa, K. Triterpenoids from Euphorbia maculata and Their Anti-Inflammatory Effects. Molecules 2018, 23, 2112. <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules23092112</nowiki></ref>
Additionally, the sap can be ingested to act as a [[laxative]] or to induce vomiting. It can also be used topically to treat sores, [[lesions]], [[warts]], and soreness.<ref> Korchmal, Arnold & Connie. 1973. A Guide to the Medicinal Plants of the United States. The New York Times Book Company, New York.</ref>

== Toxicity ==
''Euphorbia maculata,'' like much of the Euphorbiaceae is considered toxic. Its effects may include mild skin irritation, which is amplified when exposed to the sun, irritation to the stomach, and vomiting as well as being generally considered a carcinogen.<ref>Miller, Candice. "Plants That Cause Skin Irritation" (PDF). ''University     of Illinois Extension''. Archived from the original (PDF) on 1 July 2015. Retrieved 18 September 2014.</ref> The toxins come from a thin, white, milky sap that is produced when either the leaf or the stem gets broken. Contact with the eyes, skin, or mouth should be avoided.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Keep Away From Spurge Sap |url=https://www.poison.org/articles/keep-away-from-spurge-sap-222 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=www.poison.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Weed control ==
Because ''Euphorbia maculata'' grows quickly in a variety of climates it is seen as a weed throughout much of North America and can be a particularly troublesome weed in crop fields and pastures. The growth of ''E.{{nbsp}}maculata'' in agricultural fields may impact crops yields such as vegetables, legumes, and cereals. Due to toxicity, the growth of ''Euphorbia maculata'' in pastures can cause sickness, vomiting, and weakness in livestock.<ref>Tanveer, A., et al. "Implications of weeds of genus euphorbia for crop production: a review." ''Planta Daninha'' 31 (2013): 723-731.</ref> 

Pre-emergence herbicides are useful where problems have been known to arise and mulching is not possible.<ref>"Spotted Spurge, Chamaesyce (=Euphorbia) maculata". ''Wisconsin Horticulture''. Retrieved 2024-10-24</ref> Mechanical control is hand pulling of the entire plant, roots included, to prevent regrowth. Another non-chemical control method is to apply a thick layer of mulch to the affected area. Spotted Spurge grows best in open, sunny areas, so mulching with a layer wood chips or straw prevent may smother the plant.<ref name=":1" />

30 percent vinegar is also an effective and nontoxic herbicide for Spurge Weed as well as many other common weeds.{{cn|date=October 2025}}
